summary: Brittany Walker (CRV) moderates a panel with Chris White (Prefect CTO) and Bryan Bischof (Hex Head of AI) on pivoting established startups toward AI. Chris explains Prefect's motivation: AI workloads are data-driven, and AI in production is fundamentally a remote API that is expensive, brittle, and non-deterministic—essentially a data API that Prefect can orchestrate. Prefect created the open-source Marvin project to learn without full commitment; all upside if it fails, valuable connections if it succeeds. Bryan argues any data platform not integrating AI is dooming itself, and his team charter is making Hex feel magical. Both companies kept AI teams deliberately lean—Hex has ~5 engineers despite a roadmap for 20—through ruthless prioritization. On build vs buy, Hex built its own evaluation infrastructure because evals must be as close to production as possible, and built a custom LanceDB-based retrieval implementation for a complex RAG pipeline. Prefect built all AI tooling in-house. Post-rollout, Bryan 'drinks his own champagne,' using Magic daily and even using Magic to analyze Magic's performance through traditional product analytics. Chris describes testing typed outputs via Marvin's type-guaranteed handshakes, making LLM outputs testable. Bryan's eval philosophy is emphatically binary: boil tasks down to yes/no judgments rather than latent distance distributions or BLEU scores, and for those who say their task is too complex, 'try harder.' Model degradation is real—Bryan's evals caught endpoint changes before he even switched endpoints. For agent pipelines, Chris stresses failure-mode thinking, observability, caching, and monitoring of returned code. Bryan addressed hallucination by building a better custom retrieval mechanism rather than following generic RAG guidance. Closing hot takes: Chris says stop building chat interfaces—AI is a tool, not a product, and machine-to-machine integration matters more. Bryan warns that building AI capabilities involves incredibly boring data engineering work that people haven't yet appreciated, but the tedious journey is worth it.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Backgrounds
sections.summary: Brittany Walker (CRV) introduces the panel. Chris White (Prefect CTO) has a math PhD in non-convex optimization and builds workflow orchestration tooling. Bryan Bischof leads AI at Hex, a data science notebook platform, with a math PhD and a decade in data science and ML.

sections.title: Deciding to Invest in AI
sections.summary: Chris explains Prefect's motivation: AI workloads are data-driven, and AI in production is a remote API that is expensive, brittle, and non-deterministic—essentially a data API. Prefect created the open-source Marvin project to learn in the open. Bryan argues any data platform not integrating AI is dooming itself, and AI unlocks creativity and business acumen in data science workflows.

sections.title: Criteria for Building AI Features
sections.summary: Chris describes two tracks: Marvin (open-source, success = learning from users) and core product AI features (failure-mode thinking, quick error summaries, measuring how quickly users debug). Bryan's charter is making Hex feel magical, citing an explode feature that splits long SQL CTEs into chained cells.

sections.title: Resource Allocation and Team Building
sections.summary: Bryan started with one hacker, built a prototype, and scaled to ~5 engineers despite a roadmap for 20, emphasizing ruthless prioritization. Prefect hired Adam to own AI, plus one engineer who switched full-time to Adam's team.

sections.title: Measuring Success
sections.summary: Chris reports time-to-value improvements in core product and regular early conversations with companies productionizing AI. Bryan measures success by how frequently users reach for Magic across all parts of Hex's platform, making it a North Star to have AI assistance in every platform aspect.

sections.title: Build vs Buy: Evals and Vector Databases
sections.summary: Bryan prioritized evaluation from day one (February 2023), building evals in-house because they must be as close to production as possible. Hex chose not to build its own vector database, instead building a custom LanceDB-based retrieval implementation for a complex RAG pipeline. Chris says Prefect built all AI tooling in-house since they already had sufficient dev tooling for observability and monitoring, with no buying at all.

sections.title: Infrastructure Wishes and Gaps
sections.summary: Bryan says it would have been hard to sell him on an eval platform, but sees opportunity for an LLM observability platform combining experimentation. He is watching Rivet by Ironclad, an open-source library for experimentation and iteration. Chris wants more focus on machine-to-machine AI tooling, particularly guaranteed typed output via function calling to integrate AI into backend processes.

sections.title: Production Challenges
sections.summary: Chris says tooling-wise AI integration was smooth, but culturally engineers wanted AI to do everything—restraining enthusiasm was the biggest challenge, requiring focus on specific areas like removing user friction. Bryan found estimation with AI features is exacerbated: initial experiments show great promise quickly but the long tail to bulletproof production feels even longer than typical engineering corner-case triage.

sections.title: Testing and Tracking
sections.summary: Bryan emphasizes robust evals and codifying feature requests into evaluations. When users suggest Magic should do X, his team probes what they expect and uses a barometer: could a new data scientist at the company with very little context accomplish that task, defining the cutting edge of what's feasible.

sections.title: Separate vs Integrated AI Products
sections.summary: Chris explains Marvin was started as a separate open-source repo to maximize learning without full commitment—all upside with minimal maintenance cost. For core product AI, Prefect focused on marginal adds since as a general-purpose orchestrator, helping write arbitrary code adds no value over OpenAI or GitHub. Bryan emphasizes Magic is not a product but an augmentation of Hex, making the platform easier and more comfortable to use.

sections.title: UX and Rollout Strategy
sections.summary: Bryan describes killing a Crystal Ball feature that worked beautifully but pulled users away from the core Hex experience, reinforcing that Magic must augment, not split, the platform. Rollout starts with a private beta, then expands to public beta as quickly as possible, targeting engaged users prepared for AI's stochasticity and limitations.

sections.title: Rollout, Security, and Enterprise Considerations
sections.summary: Bryan describes targeting technical users first in early rollout, then scaling to include the broader distribution of technical capabilities. Marvin's public release was casual—hacking on it, feeling proud, clicking make public, tweeting. For core product AI, Chris notes Prefect's large enterprise, financial services, and healthcare customers required opt-in features with clear data disclosure about third-party providers.

sections.title: Post-Rollout Measurement
sections.summary: Bryan 'drinks his own champagne'—using Magic daily and using Magic to analyze Magic's performance through traditional product analytics. Chris describes early testing using LLMs for semantic comparisons, then transitioning to typed output testing via Marvin's type-guaranteed handshakes, making LLM outputs straightforward to test.

sections.title: Evaluation Philosophy and Model Drift
sections.summary: Bryan references a paper about models degrading over time and notes his evals caught endpoint changes before he even switched endpoints. His eval philosophy: boil tasks to binary yes/no judgments, avoid latent distance distributions, KL divergence, and BLEU scores. For those who claim their task is too complex for binary evals, he challenges them to 'try harder.' Chris notes these non-deterministic, dynamic experimentation workflows are exactly what Prefect's core product is built for.

sections.title: Cross-Questions: Agent Pipelines and Hallucination
sections.summary: Bryan asks Chris about agent pipelines and DAGs. Chris's main advice: think about failure modes—runaway processes, capturing oddities early via observability, monitoring returned code, and caching (which is both friend and root of all evil). Chris asks Bryan about hallucination. Bryan found that better custom retrieval design reduced hallucination, noting the retrieval mechanism took additional thinking and isn't found in any book, including his own.

sections.title: Closing Hot Takes
sections.summary: Chris's hot take: stop building chat interfaces—AI is a tool, not a product; focus on machine-to-machine interfaces so developers can use AI more directly. Bryan's hot take: the work building AI capabilities is going to be incredibly boring data engineering, and people haven't appreciated how important that is, but the tedious journey is worth it in the end.
